claim: Kinase activity in signaling networks frequently depends on regulatory subunits that can both inhibit activity by interacting with the catalytic subunits and target the kinase to distinct molecular partners and subcellular compartments.
source: Kinase activity in signaling networks frequently depends on regulatory subunits that can both inhibit activity by interacting with the catalytic subunits and target the kinase to distinct molecular partners and subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinase regulation that draws from established scientific understanding of kinase function.

claim: Translocation of PKA-R to the plasma membrane can enhance membrane kinase activity at lower translocation levels, even in the absence of signaling inputs.
source: Here, using a new synthetic molecular interaction system, we show that translocation of a regulatory subunit of the protein kinase A (PKA-R) to the plasma membrane has a paradoxical effect on the membrane kinase activity. It can both enhance it at lower translocation levels, even in the absence of signaling inputs, and inhibit it at higher translocation levels, suggesting its role as a linker that can both couple and decouple signaling processes in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the FRET biosensor experiments showing PKA activity increases upon PKA-R translocation.

claim: Translocation of PKA-R to the plasma membrane can inhibit membrane kinase activity at higher translocation levels.
source: Here, using a new synthetic molecular interaction system, we show that translocation of a regulatory subunit of the protein kinase A (PKA-R) to the plasma membrane has a paradoxical effect on the membrane kinase activity. It can both enhance it at lower translocation levels, even in the absence of signaling inputs, and inhibit it at higher translocation levels, suggesting its role as a linker that can both couple and decouple signaling processes in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing PKA activity decreases below baseline at high PKA-R expression levels.

claim: PKA-R can act as a linker that can both couple and decouple signaling processes in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: It can both enhance it at lower translocation levels, even in the absence of signaling inputs, and inhibit it at higher translocation levels, suggesting its role as a linker that can both couple and decouple signaling processes in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental observations and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Superposition of gradients of PKA-R abundance across single cells can control the directionality of cell migration.
source: We further demonstrate that superposition of gradients of PKA-R abundance across single cells can control the directionality of cell migration, reversing it at high enough input levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microfluidic gradient experiments showing cell migration reversal.

claim: Complex in vivo patterns of PKA-R localization can drive complex phenotypes, including cell migration.
source: Thus, complex in vivo patterns of PKA-R localization can drive complex phenotypes, including cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of PKA-R translocation effects on cell migration.

claim: Adapter and scaffold proteins facilitate molecular interactions by linking activated enzymes to substrates within specific subcellular compartments.
source: These interactions are facilitated by large sets of adapter and scaffold proteins linking the activated enzymes to substrates within specific subcellular compartments, controlling dynamic modifications of protein localization and local concentrations of effector molecules (Langeberg and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PKA molecules are complexes of two catalytic subunits (PKA-C) and a regulatory subunit dimer (PKA-R) that can dissociate following binding of two cyclic AMP (cAMP) molecules to each of the PKA-R subunits.
source: Instead, a PKA molecule is a complex of two catalytic subunits (PKA-C) and a regulatory subunit dimer (PKA-R) that can dissociate following binding of two cyclic AMP (cAMP) molecules to each of the PKA-R subunits (Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature describing PKA structure and function.

claim: PKA signaling complexity includes dynamically shifting subcellular pools of cAMP, tethering of the kinase and its substrates to A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs), localized phosphatase and phosphodiesterase activity, and the intrinsic inhibitory function of PKA-R.
source: This intricate organization of the kinase complex is further complicated by dynamically shifting subcellular pools of cAMP, tethering of the kinase and its substrates to a large family of differentially localized A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs), localized phosphatase and phosphodiesterase activity, and the intrinsic inhibitory function of PKA-R (Baillie, 2009; Wong and Scott, 2004; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A scaffold protein can enhance pathway activity at an optimal level but can also inhibit it if its concentration exceeds the optimum.
source: It has been shown, for example, for the MAPK signaling pathways, that a scaffold protein can enhance the pathway activity at an optimal level but can also inhibit it if its concentration exceeds the optimum (Chapman and Asthagiri, 2009; Levchenko et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on scaffold protein effects.

claim: Variation of the relative abundance of pathway components can modulate pathway activity even if the input levels do not change.
source: This 'combinatorial inhibition' effect (Good et al., 2011) suggests that variation of the relative abundance of the pathway components can modulate the pathway activity even if the input levels do not change.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference from the combinatorial inhibition concept.

claim: Compartmentalized PKA signaling is important in glucose homeostasis, cardiomyocyte contractility, cell cycle regulation, and cell migration.
source: Compartmentalized PKA signaling is important in a number of contexts including glucose homeostasis, cardiomyocyte contractility, cell cycle regulation, and cell migration (Howe, 2004; Langeberg and Scott, 2005; Mauban et al., 2009; Wong and Scott, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PKA positively affects the activity of some cytoskeletal regulators (e.g., Rac1, Cdc42, α4β1 integrin) and negatively affects others (e.g., RhoA).
source: In regulating cell migration, PKA is known to positively affect the activity of some cytoskeletal regulators (e.g., Rac1, Cdc42, α4β1 integrin) and negatively affect others (e.g., RhoA).
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about PKA's effects on cytoskeletal regulators.

claim: Both inhibition and activation of PKA have been shown to have inhibitory effects on cell migration.
source: Additionally, both inhibition and activation of PKA have been shown to have inhibitory effects on cell migration (Howe, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several studies utilizing FRET biosensors have identified gradients of PKA activity in migrating cells, with relatively high PKA activity at the cell front and relatively low activity at the rear.
source: Several studies utilizing FRET biosensors have identified gradients of PKA activity in migrating cells, with relatively high PKA activity at the cell front and relatively low activity at the rear, suggesting that spatial control of the kinase is involved in this process (Lim et al., 2008; Paulucci-Holthauzen et al., 2009; Tkachenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The regulatory but not the catalytic subunit of PKA has been shown to be enriched in the pseudopods of cells in culture.
source: Furthermore, the regulatory but not the catalytic subunit has been shown to be enriched in the pseudopods of cells in culture, suggesting that regulatory subunit localization may play a role in the regulation of cell migration (Howe et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Of the four PKA-R isoforms (PKAR-Iα/β, PKAR-IIα, and PKAR-IIβ) in a standard HeLa cell line, the expression of PKAR-IIβ was particularly low.
source: We found that of the four PKA-R isoforms (PKAR-Iα/β, PKAR-IIα, and PKAR-IIβ) in a standard HeLa cell line, the expression of PKAR-IIβ was particularly low (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and D, rightmost lane), prompting us to use this isoform as the basis for development of the chemical dimerization-based tool for acutely controlling local PKA-R abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rapamycin induces heterodimerization of FKBP and FRB.
source: Rapamycin induces dimerization of two small, intracellularly transduced molecular components: FK506-binding protein (FKBP) and the FKPB-rapamycin domain (FRB), which can be tethered to proteins of interest as well as specific subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rapamycin-induced dimerization systems.

claim: Transfection of the modified PKAR-IIβ changed the expression level of this subunit in both transiently transfected cells (to a lower degree) and stably transfected clones (to a greater degree).
source: Although, expectedly, transfection of the modified PKAR-IIβ changed the expression level of this subunit in both transiently transfected (to a lower degree) cells and stably transfected clones (to a greater degree), the expression of PKA-C and most other isoforms was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of PKA-C and most other PKA-R isoforms was not affected by transfection of the modified PKAR-IIβ.
source: Although, expectedly, transfection of the modified PKAR-IIβ changed the expression level of this subunit in both transiently transfected (to a lower degree) cells and stably transfected clones (to a greater degree), the expression of PKA-C and most other isoforms was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The localization of the modified PKAR-IIβ was confined to the cytosol prior to stimulation.
source: the localization of the modified PKAR-IIβ was confined to the cytosol prior to stimulation (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no detectable phenotypic effect of induced expression of modified PKAR-IIβ.
source: the localization of the modified PKAR-IIβ was confined to the cytosol prior to stimulation (Figure 1C) and there was no detectable phenotypic effect of this induced expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, representing a negative result.

claim: Addition of rapamycin resulted in rapid PKA-R translocation to the plasma membrane evaluated as a significant decrease in the cytoplasmic fluorescence intensity over the first 3 min of stimulation.
source: Addition of rapamycin resulted in rapid PKA-R translocation to the PM evaluated as a significant decrease in the cytoplasmic fluorescence intensity over the first 3 min of stimulation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: No significant PKA-R translocation occurred after the initial 3 minute period following rapamycin addition.
source: No significant translocation occurred after this initial period.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 1D showing plateau of translocation.

claim: PKA-C translocated to the cell membrane along with exogenous PKA-R following rapamycin addition.
source: Following addition of rapamycin, PKA-C indeed translocated to the cell membrane whereas mCherry alone underwent no significant change in localization, demonstrating that our synthetic system can bring the intact PKA holoenzyme to the PM (Figure 1E and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: mCherry protein alone underwent no significant change in localization following rapamycin addition.
source: Following addition of rapamycin, PKA-C indeed translocated to the cell membrane whereas mCherry alone underwent no significant change in localization, demonstrating that our synthetic system can bring the intact PKA holoenzyme to the PM (Figure 1E and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E serving as a negative control.

claim: HeLa cells expressing PKAR-FKBP-FP and treated with rapamycin displayed a rapid change in cell morphology (spreading) and an increase in filopodia formation.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to absence of any detectable phenotypic effect of PKAR-FKBP-FP expression in unstimulated HeLa cells, these cells treated with rapamycin displayed a rapid change in cell morphology (spreading) and an increase in filopodia formation (not observed in untransfected cells treated with the same rapamycin dose) (Figure 1C and Video 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: The dynamic range of intracellular Lyn-AKAR4 responses in HeLa PFM cells was determined to be 20.9% ± 2.0% (n = 12) following cell treatment with forskolin and IBMX.
source: The dynamic range of the intracellular Lyn-AKAR4 responses in this cell line was determined to be 20.9% ± 2.0% (n = 12) (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM] [n = number of cells]) following cell treatment with a combination of an adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (Fsk, 50 μM) and a competitive non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX, 100 μM) to maximally increase the intracellular cAMP levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET biosensor data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rapamycin-induced PKA-R translocation alone (without any additional stimulation) was able to induce a significant increase in PKA activity.
source: Surprisingly, we found that rapamycin-induced PKA-R translation alone (without any additional stimulation) was able to induce a significant increase in PKA activity, which was transient in some cells and sustained in others (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET biosensor data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The increase in PKA activity following PKA-R translocation was greatest for cells with intermediate PKA-R concentrations, decreasing when PKA-R was either higher or lower than this optimal level.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the increase in activity was greatest for cells with intermediate PKA-R concentrations, decreasing when PKA-R was either higher or lower than this optimal level (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C correlating PKA-R concentration with PKA activity.

claim: In cells with the highest PKA-R expression, PKA activity, following the initial rise, later not only decreased vs. the maximum, but dropped below the basal level, indicating active inhibition of the PKA activity.
source: Furthermore, in the cells with the highest PKA-R expression, PKA activity, following the initial rise, later not only decreased vs. the maximum, but dropped below the basal level, indicating active inhibition of the PKA activity (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E showing PKA activity dynamics in high PKA-R expressing cells.

claim: Treatment of cells with 20 nM of rapamycin led to PKA activation that was, on average, transient.
source: We again found that treatment of cells with 20 nM of rapamycin led to PKA activation that was, on average, transient, consistent with the gradual accumulation of PKA-R at the PM, first to optimal and then inhibitory levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Inducing a decreased level of PKA-R translocation with 2 nM rapamycin resulted in a slower but much more sustained increase in PKA activity, reaching, on average, much higher levels than those seen for the higher dose.
source: Importantly, we found that inducing a decreased level of PKA-R translocation with a lower dose of rapamycin (2 nM) resulted in a slower but much more sustained increase in PKA activity, reaching, on average, much higher levels than those seen for the higher dose (Figure 2F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F comparing different rapamycin doses.

claim: PKA-R translocation to the PM can stimulate the PKA activity up to an optimal level of this subunit but can also inhibit PKA when the PKA-R levels exceed the optimal level in the PM compartment.
source: These results collectively suggested that PKA-R translocation to the PM can stimulate the PKA activity up to an optimal level of this subunit but can also inhibit PKA when the PKA-R levels exceed the optimal level in the PM compartment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Similar to linker or scaffold molecules, PKA-R can both enhance and inhibit signaling output, depending on its concentration relative to the concentrations of the other components of the holoenzyme.
source: To account for this paradoxical effect of the local PKA-R abundance, we hypothesized that similar to linker or scaffold molecules, this subunit can both enhance and inhibit signaling output, depending on its concentration relative to the concentrations of the other components of the holoenzyme (e.g., cAMP or PKA-C molecules).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: A mathematical model suggests that there is an optimal level of concentration expected for PKA-R, if it behaves as a linker molecule.
source: We constructed a new heuristic mathematical model of this effect, which, along with our prior modeling effort (Levchenko et al., 2000), suggested that there is indeed an optimal level of concentration expected for PKA-R, if it behaves as such a linker molecule (Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling described in Appendix 1 and cited prior work.

claim: An increase in the local PKA-R abundance was predicted to potentially drive the signaling to below baseline levels, if the initial concentration of PKA-R at the PM was sufficiently high prior to forced PKA-R translocation.
source: Furthermore, an increase in the local PKA-R abundance was predicted to potentially drive the signaling to below baseline levels, if the initial concentration of PKA-R at the PM was sufficiently high prior to forced PKA-R translocation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model.

claim: Rapamycin-based PKA-R translocation to the PM leads to a gradual accumulation of this PKA subunit in the specific subcellular compartment, allowing it to progressively accumulate at sub-optimal, optimal, and supra-optimal levels.
source: Overall, the combination of experimental and mathematical analyses suggested that rapamycin-based PKA-R translocation to the PM leads to a gradual accumulation of this PKA subunit in the specific subcellular compartment, allowing it to progressively accumulate at sub-optimal, optimal, and supra-optimal levels, and thus initially enhance and then inhibit signaling output, by virtue of serving the role of a linker in the holoenzyme complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: PKA activity and PKA-R abundance have been shown to be elevated at the front of migrating cells in vitro.
source: PKA activity and PKA-R abundance have been shown to be elevated at the front of migrating cells in vitro, but the role that spatial localization of PKA plays in regulating cell migration is not well understood (Lim et al., 2008; Paulucci-Holthauzen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Upon application of a rapamycin gradient (0–20 nM, 0.08 nM/μm), there was a pronounced reversal of the directionality of the cells' migration in the direction opposite to the initial 'upward' bias.
source: Upon application of a rapamycin gradient (0–20 nM, 0.08 nM/μm), we found a pronounced reversal of the directionality of the cells' migration in the direction opposite to the initial 'upward' bias, with the preferred new direction thus being opposite to the direction of the rapamycin gradient (Figure 3C and E and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 3C and E and Video 3.

claim: Cells without expression of Lyn-FRB or cells exposed to a DMSO gradient did not experience PKA-R translocation and continued migrating in the 'upward' direction.
source: This was in stark contrast to cells without expression of Lyn-FRB or cells exposed to a DMSO gradient that did not experience PKA-R translocation and continued migrating in the 'upward' direction (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 4.

claim: Prior to rapamycin exposure, most cells displayed an internal PKA activity gradient that corresponded with the cell polarization state (high PKA activity at the cell front and low at the rear).
source: Prior to rapamycin exposure, most cells displayed an internal PKA activity gradient that corresponded with the cell polarization state (high PKA activity at the cell front and low at the rear) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Upon exposure to the rapamycin gradient, a reversal in the direction of the internal PKA activity gradient was observed that was concurrent with the flip in the direction of cell migration.
source: Upon exposure to the rapamycin gradient, we observed a reversal in the direction of the internal PKA activity gradient that was concurrent with the flip in the direction of cell migration (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: A transient increase in PKA activity at the cell front was observed prior to the reversal of the internal PKA activity gradient.
source: Interestingly, we also observed a transient increase in PKA activity at the cell front (Figure 3F, 15 min time point) prior to this reversal.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 3F at the 15 min time point.

claim: A spatially uniform 20 nM rapamycin concentration had no detectable effect on cell migration directionality.
source: We found that whereas the lower rapamycin concentration had no detectable effect (vs. e.g., the control Figure 3D), the higher concentration gradually randomized the cell migration directionality, suggesting a stronger negating effect on the intrinsic polarity regulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A spatially uniform 100 nM rapamycin concentration gradually randomized the cell migration directionality.
source: We found that whereas the lower rapamycin concentration had no detectable effect (vs. e.g., the control Figure 3D), the higher concentration gradually randomized the cell migration directionality, suggesting a stronger negating effect on the intrinsic polarity regulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: A shallow rapamycin gradient (10 nM – 20 nM across the channel, or 0.04 nM/μm) resulted in reversal of the average migration directionality.
source: We then exposed the cells to a relatively shallow rapamycin gradient (10 nM – 20 nM across the channel, or 0.04 nM/μm), contrasting the results with those produced by steeper spatially graded stimulation (0–20 nM, or 0.08 nM/μm, Figure 3E). We again found reversal of the average migration directionality, which was increasingly more pronounced with increasing gradient slope (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: The reversal of migration directionality was increasingly more pronounced with increasing rapamycin gradient slope.
source: We again found reversal of the average migration directionality, which was increasingly more pronounced with increasing gradient slope (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 4D and F comparing different gradient slopes.

claim: Presenting cells with a reverse rapamycin gradient (20–0 nM, 'downward') resulted in most cells moving similarly to the control case, while a subset of cells reversed their directionality from 'downward' to 'upward', and another subset displayed an increased speed of 'upward' migration.
source: We indeed observed that most cells under this condition moved similarly to the control case, while a subset of cells reversed their directionality from 'downward' to 'upward', and another subset displayed an increased speed of 'upward' migration vs. the maximal cell migration levels observed in the control (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Relocalization of PKA-R to the PM was sufficient to induce an increase in PKA activity in this intracellular compartment, particularly for lower levels of the translocated PKA-R, even in the absence of changes in upstream signaling through G protein-coupled receptors.
source: We demonstrate in particular that relocalization of PKA-R to the PM was sufficient to induce an increase in PKA activity in this intracellular compartment, particularly for lower levels of the translocated PKA-R, even in the absence of changes in upstream signaling through G protein-coupled receptors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of the PKA-R translocation reached the maximal level at the optimum level of this subunit, decreasing at PKA-R higher levels and ultimately driving the PKA activity to below basal levels.
source: The effect of the PKA-R translocation reached the maximal level at the optimum level of this subunit, decreasing at PKA-R higher levels and ultimately driving the PKA activity to below basal levels.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At low levels, a scaffold can enhance signaling by bringing components of a signaling pathway into close proximity, enabling their interaction, and thus enhancing the pathway activity.
source: At low levels, a scaffold can enhance signaling by bringing components of a signaling pathway into close proximity, enabling their interaction, and thus enhancing the pathway activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about scaffold protein function, supported by citations earlier in the text.

claim: When the scaffold concentration is too high, it sequesters pathway components away from each other, decreasing the pathway activity.
source: However, when the scaffold concentration is too high, it sequesters pathway components away from each other, decreasing the pathway activity, a behavior that is recapitulated by our mathematical model.
evidence: This is established knowledge about scaffold protein function, supported by citations earlier in the text and the mathematical model.

claim: Within the cell, PKA-R plays a scaffold-like role for PKA-C and cAMP since the kinase activity requires linkage of two PKA-C subunits and four cAMP molecules into one molecular complex by these subunits.
source: Our results suggest that within the cell, PKA-R plays a scaffold-like role for PKA-C and cAMP since the kinase activity requires linkage of two PKA-C subunits and four cAMP molecules into one molecular complex by these subunits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of known PKA structure.

claim: When the local PKA-R concentration is too high, it can lead to incomplete binding (titration away) of either cAMP or PKA-C, preventing activation.
source: When the local PKA-R concentration is too high, it can lead to incomplete binding (titration away) of either cAMP or PKA-C, preventing activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: As PKA-R is recruited to the membrane, PKA activity will increase until there is a local shortage of one or both of these components (cAMP or PKA-C).
source: Therefore, as PKA-R is recruited to the membrane, PKA activity will increase until there is a local shortage of one or both of these components.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: PKA-R can have either a pathway inhibitory or enhancing role, depending on the expression of PKA-C or cAMP abundance both globally across the cell and in specific subcellular compartments.
source: This suggests a more complex view of PKA-R's role in this pathway, suggesting that it can have either a pathway inhibitory or enhancing role, depending on the expression of PKA-C or cAMP abundance both globally across the cell and in specific subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: The abundance of PKA-R at the PM in the HeLa cells investigated is sub-optimal.
source: In particular, our results suggest that the abundance of PKA-R at the PM in the HeLa cells investigated here is sub-optimal, but one can expect that it can be optimal or 'super-optimal' in other cellular compartments.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations showing that PKA-R translocation increases PKA activity.

claim: Inducing gradients of PKA-R PM translocation at levels inhibitory to PKA activity led to a reversal of the internal PKA activity gradient and, as a result, the cell polarity and direction of cell migration.
source: We indeed found that inducing gradients of PKA-R PM translocation at levels inhibitory to PKA activity led to a reversal of the internal PKA activity gradient and, as a result, the cell polarity and direction of cell migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the microfluidic gradient experiments.

claim: This work demonstrates for the first time that intracellular PKA activity gradients can provide a polarization cue that is powerful enough to overcome other existing polarization cues inside the cell.
source: This work therefore demonstrates for the first time that intracellular PKA activity gradients can provide a polarization cue that is powerful enough to overcome other existing polarization cues inside the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell migration reversal experiments.

claim: PKA activity gradients likely exert an effect on cell polarization via modulation of the activity of the two mutually inhibitory Rho-family small GTPases RhoA and Rac1.
source: It is likely that PKA activity gradients exert an effect on cell polarization via modulation of the activity of the two mutually inhibitory Rho-family small GTPases RhoA and Rac1.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation based on known PKA targets.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of RhoA on Ser188 has been shown to promote its interaction with RhoGDI, leading to removal of RhoA from the PM.
source: PKA phosphorylation of RhoA on Ser188 has been shown to promote its interaction with RhoGDI, leading to removal of RhoA from the PM (Lang et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PKA is implicated in Rac1 activation, although the direct target of this positive regulation is still unclear.
source: PKA is also implicated in Rac1 activation, although the direct target of this positive regulation is still unclear (O'Connor and Mercurio, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PKA has a positive effect on Rac1 activity and a negative effect on membrane localized RhoA activity.
source: Since PKA has a positive effect on Rac1 activity and a negative effect on membrane localized RhoA activity, it would be reasonable to theorize that PKA acts to shift the balance of Rac1 to RhoA signaling in favor of Rac1.
evidence: This is a summary of known PKA effects on these GTPases, supported by citations earlier in the text.

claim: A gradient of intracellular PKA activity could help to enhance the internal polarization of Rac1 and RhoA.
source: In this way, a gradient of intracellular PKA activity could help to enhance the internal polarization of these two polarity effectors.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for how PKA gradients affect cell polarity.

claim: When the PKA activity gradient flips, the effect would be to increase Rac1 and decrease RhoA activity at the cell rear, leading to a reversal of polarity if this signal is sufficiently strong.
source: When the PKA activity gradient flips, as in Figure 3G, the effect would be to increase Rac1 and decrease RhoA activity at the cell rear, leading to a reversal of polarity if this signal is sufficiently strong.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed polarity reversal.

claim: The subcellular kinase concentration can be tuned by the expression levels of various scaffold proteins.
source: In a broader sense, this work demonstrates the critical role that kinase localization plays in controlling the cell response to an incoming stimulus. The subcellular kinase concentration can be tuned by the expression levels of various scaffold proteins, and differential expression between cells may result in variability of signaling responses within a population.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Differential expression of scaffold proteins between cells may result in variability of signaling responses within a population.
source: The subcellular kinase concentration can be tuned by the expression levels of various scaffold proteins, and differential expression between cells may result in variability of signaling responses within a population.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Localization of scaffold proteins may vary dynamically via modifications to subcellular localization sequences.
source: Localization of scaffold proteins may vary dynamically via modifications to subcellular localization sequences as well, resulting in similar effects to those described here.
evidence: This is a general principle based on known mechanisms of protein localization.

claim: AKAPs are receiving attention as potential therapeutic targets.
source: In the context of PKA, AKAPs are receiving attention as potential therapeutic targets, and at least one isoform of PKA-R has been implicated as a driver of oncogenesis (Codina et al., 2019; Esseltine and Scott, 2013; Veugelers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At least one isoform of PKA-R has been implicated as a driver of oncogenesis.
source: In the context of PKA, AKAPs are receiving attention as potential therapeutic targets, and at least one isoform of PKA-R has been implicated as a driver of oncogenesis (Codina et al., 2019; Esseltine and Scott, 2013; Veugelers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The kinase relocalization strategy demonstrated can be applied to study the effects of localized PKA activity in other subcellular compartments.
source: The kinase relocalization strategy demonstrated herein can be applied to study the effects of localized PKA activity in other subcellular compartments and can be adapted to the study of other kinases, enabling a better understanding of the role of compartmentalized signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the developed tool.

claim: The kinase relocalization strategy can be adapted to the study of other kinases.
source: The kinase relocalization strategy demonstrated herein can be applied to study the effects of localized PKA activity in other subcellular compartments and can be adapted to the study of other kinases, enabling a better understanding of the role of compartmentalized signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the developed tool.

claim: The rapamycin-based dimerization strategy has been used to study biochemical activity of different proteins.
source: This technique has been used to study biochemical activity of different proteins (Chu et al., 2014; Dagliyan et al., 2017; Dagliyan et al., 2013; Inoue et al., 2005; Karginov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The dimerization strategy, when combined with the use of a microfluidic device controlling spatial rapamycin distribution, can be used to study biomolecular systems controlling cell polarity and migration.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that this dimerization strategy, when combined with the use of a microfluidic device controlling spatial rapamycin distribution, can be used to study biomolecular systems controlling cell polarity and migration (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.
